query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) coating can protect hot dip aluminum plating equipment from erosion during long-term exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy engineered with coherent nanoprecipitates that deliver ultra-high strength and stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a coating or fabricate parts from the tungsten-based RHEA on components (e.g., sinking rollers, pulling rollers, guide plates) exposed to liquid aluminum.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature (around 660 °C) liquid aluminum during the hot dip plating process over extended operational periods.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of coherent nanoprecipitates within the RHEA microstructure, which enhance both strength and stability, and provide chemical inertness with respect to liquid aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten-based RHEA’s high melting point and corrosion resistance reduce the tendency for aluminum to react with the material. Its stable microstructure—with coherent nanoprecipitates—limits the formation of detrimental intermetallic phases and minimizes erosion by resisting chemical attack by liquid aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated or fabricated parts will exhibit significantly reduced corrosion and erosion, thereby extending the service life of the dipping and plating equipment relative to components made from conventional materials (e.g., standard steels or nickel-based alloys).
generation.baseline: Current equipment manufactured from conventional alloys typically suffers from rapid degradation due to the corrosive nature of high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: While the RHEA is expected to perform well at 660 °C, uncertainties remain regarding its adhesion to substrates over long periods, the influence of thermal cycling, and potential processing challenges during application.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in erosion resistance and long-term durability under cyclic thermal stresses has not been fully established and requires further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of dipping and plating equipment parts coated with the tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy and subject them to a controlled hot dip aluminum bath test at approximately 660 °C for an extended duration (e.g., 200–300 hours). In parallel, test identical parts made from conventional alloys under the same conditions.
measurements: Weight loss and mass gain measurements over time
Surface morphology and microstructural analysis using SEM and XRD before and after exposure
Mechanical property testing (hardness, tensile strength) pre- and post-exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-based RHEA-coated parts do not show statistically significant improvement in resistance to erosion (i.e., similar or greater weight loss, surface degradation, or loss in mechanical integrity) compared to conventional materials, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
